explanations: terra: Israel is rescued from Pharaoh's people, who imposed terrible torment, slaughtered sons, and spared women, showing the bodily reality of oppressive mastery.
terra: Hearts become like stones or harder, while even stones split, release water, or fall in awe; the image exposes a hardness less responsive than rock.

luna: This covenant joins kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy with وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا. It places good speech beside care for the vulnerable, as the section joins the orphan and asker to gentle treatment. | terra: The covenant places good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, and the needy beside وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا, gathering the section's vulnerable recipients and gentle speech.

luna: This verse joins spending wealth on orphans, needy people, travelers, and السَّائِلِينَ to faith and care. The shared vulnerable recipients connect the section's gift and its refusal to rebuke the asker. | terra: True devotion includes giving loved wealth to kin, orphans, the needy, traveler, and askers, so the section's orphan and asker both meet an open hand.
terra: God explicitly intends ease for people and does not intend hardship in the fasting law, stating the divine preference that the section perceives through its soft roots.
terra: When servants ask about God, He answers that He is near and responds to the caller who calls, making attentive reception the divine answer to asking.
terra: The answer about spending names parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers, directing material giving toward the same vulnerable relations developed in the section.

luna: Asked about orphans, the verse answers that their improvement is best and calls them brothers. It gives a constructive relation to the orphan that counters the section's prohibition on overpowering him. | terra: Orphans are to be met through reform and fraternity, and God says He could have burdened people had He willed; the ayah opposes exploitative handling with brotherly care and divine forbearance.
terra: Marriage may be retained بِمَعْرُوفٍ or released بِإِحْسَانٍ; even literal social holding and letting go are bounded by the section's gentle grip.
terra: وَلَا تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرَارًا forbids retaining wives in order to harm and transgress; literal holding becomes unlawful when used as pressure.
terra: The invitation to lend generously is followed by وَاللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْسُطُ; constriction and expansion become explicit divine “holds” around human giving.
terra: The ark's sign includes سَكِينَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ, giving the exact calm named by the section's dictionary gloss a divinely sent, tangible bearer.
terra: There is no compulsion in religion, yet the believer grasps the firmest handhold; secure holding is distinguished from coercive force in one ayah.

luna: Continuing the charity passage around 2:263, this verse says spenders do not follow their giving with reminders or injury. Its own contribution is to keep a gift from turning into a verbal or emotional burden. | terra: Giving remains sound only when it is not followed by reminder or injury; this supplies the rule whose verbal alternative is stated in 2:263.

luna: The section cites this contrast: قَوْلٌ مَعْرُوفٌ وَمَغْفِرَةٌ is better than charity followed by أَذًى. A gift loses its kindness when the giver adds injury. | terra: قَوْلٌ مَعْرُوفٌ وَمَغْفِرَةٌ is better than charity followed by hurt, so a soft word can outweigh a gift made into a second form of hard handling.

luna: The next verse warns that reminders and injury can nullify charity. It completes 2:263's boundary: giving cannot justify the hard treatment the section forbids. | terra: The ban on nullifying charity through reminders and injury completes 2:262–263: a materially open hand is still hard if it humiliates its recipient afterward.

luna: The needy described here avoid persistent asking, so they are easy to overlook; this is not the same as the section's explicit petitioner, but it plausibly widens its concern to a less audible form of need. | terra: The poor are restrained enough that they do not ask people insistently; the ayah teaches the reader to recognize need before the asker must expose himself to rebuke.
terra: God burdens no soul beyond its capacity, expressing a divine hold calibrated to the weakness of the person held.
terra: Mary is graciously accepted, made to grow well, entrusted to Zechariah, and found with provision; divine and human care enact shelter without domination.
terra: The God-conscious spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people, uniting an open hand with control of the impulse to strike back.

luna: The section cites لِنتَ لَهُمْ as the Prophet's gentleness and says it is mercy; this verse contrasts it with a harsh, hard-hearted stance that would scatter people from around him. | terra: Divine mercy made the Prophet لِنْتَ لَهُمْ; the stated alternative, being harsh and hard-hearted, would scatter people from around him.

luna: The verse orders orphans' property returned and forbids consuming it into one's own wealth. It makes material exploitation of an orphan a concrete form of the oppressive grip the section bans. | terra: وَآتُوا الْيَتَامَى أَمْوَالَهُمْ commands the return of orphan property and forbids consuming it, replacing possessive seizure with faithful release.

luna: The verse orders provision and clothing for dependants and قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا toward them. It makes the section's soft hand both material care and decent speech. | terra: Those not ready to manage property are still to be fed and clothed from it and addressed with قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا, again joining provision to dignifying speech.

luna: Guardians must return the orphans' property when they mature and not consume it hastily beforehand. The prohibition on rushing to take it contrasts with the section's unhurried, yielding posture. | terra: Once orphans reach sound judgment, فَادْفَعُوا إِلَيْهِمْ أَمْوَالَهُمْ requires guardians to hand their wealth over rather than keep a controlling grip.

luna: The section cites the inheritance gathering where relatives, orphans, and the poor are to receive provision and قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا. Material giving and considerate speech meet in the same scene. | terra: At an estate division, relatives, orphans, and the poor receive both provision and قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا; the ayah enacts the section's paired material and verbal gentleness.

luna: After 4:8's inheritance gathering and kind speech, this verse asks people who fear leaving weak offspring to speak قَوْلًا سَدِيدًا. It extends considerate speech to children exposed to vulnerability. | terra: Those who fear leaving vulnerable children behind must fear God and speak a sound word, linking concern for weak offspring with responsible speech.

luna: Those who consume orphan property unjustly are described as swallowing fire. This starkly marks the material opposite of the section's command not to dominate an orphan. | terra: Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly are described as consuming fire, exposing the violent reality hidden inside exploitative guardianship.
terra: Compulsory possession of women and constricting them to recover gifts are forbidden, then وَعَاشِرُوهُنَّ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ supplies the humane alternative.
terra: God wishes to lighten the human burden because humanity was created weak, a direct formulation of mercifully adjusted pressure.

luna: This command to do good includes parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy in one list. It supplies a positive counterpart to the section's specific bans on crushing and rebuking vulnerable people. | terra: Worship of God is immediately joined to good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors, travelers, and dependents, mapping the social reach of the gentle hold.

luna: The verse describes oppressed men, women, and children calling for rescue from a town of wrongdoers. Their subjection gives a concrete human scene for the section's account of قهر as domination joined to humiliation.
terra: After obedience to the Messenger is tied to obedience to God, the Prophet is told he has not been sent as a guardian over those who turn away.

luna: This ruling calls for justice toward orphan girls whose prescribed rights are withheld. It specifies one way an orphan can be overpowered, extending the section's ban to unequal treatment. | terra: The ruling about vulnerable women and children ends with وَأَنْ تَقُومُوا لِلْيَتَامَى بِالْقِسْطِ, requiring active justice for orphans.
terra: God does not love public evil speech, except from one who has been wronged; the exception draws a precise boundary around restraint of the harsh tongue.
terra: God does not intend hardship in purification but intends to complete نِعْمَتَهُ; ease and the section's named blessing root occur in a single purpose clause.
terra: Hatred of a people must not drive believers away from justice, so hostility cannot license the dominating or demeaning grip.
terra: Covenant-breaking brings hardened hearts and distorted words, yet the Prophet is told to pardon and overlook, placing hard interior and gentle response together.
terra: The coming community is أَذِلَّةٍ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَعِزَّةٍ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ, marking a contextual boundary between humble tenderness and firmness.
terra: The claim that God's hand is fettered is answered with بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ يُنْفِقُ كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ, making closed and open hands explicit images of withholding and giving.

luna: The section explicitly reserves قهر for God's authority and contrasts it with Pharaoh's boast. This verse calls God الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ, grounding that boundary in divine power. | terra: وَهُوَ الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ assigns the section's domination root to God and thus grounds its claim that the servant may not assume that position over the orphan.
terra: Affliction should have brought humility, but hearts hardened instead; the ayah identifies inward hardness as resistance to corrective mercy.

luna: The source section's dictionary note for the root ق-ل-ي gives driving or herding as a secondary sense of 93:3. This verse forbids وَلَا تَطْرُدِ those who call on their Lord morning and evening, a direct reversal of driving people away. | terra: وَلَا تَطْرُدِ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ directly forbids driving away socially weak believers, matching the section's rejected image of qalā as chasing a herd.

luna: Following the ban on expelling callers in 6:52, this verse shows people questioning why the socially lowly received God's favor. It exposes status contempt as the pressure behind the exclusion the section rejects. | terra: Between the ban on expulsion and the greeting of peace, elites ask whether these low-status believers are really those God favored; the ayah identifies the contempt that produces the hard dismissal.

luna: After the prohibition on expelling the humble callers in 6:52 and the status question in 6:53, this verse tells the Prophet to greet believers with سَلَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ and names mercy. It supplies the welcoming speech that answers exclusion. | terra: Immediately after the ban on expelling worshippers in 6:52, the Prophet must greet approaching believers with peace and announce that the Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself.

luna: This repeats the section's divine-side formulation, الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ. Its context adds God's guardians over people, reinforcing the distinction between God's sovereignty and a human's abuse of the vulnerable. | terra: The repeated وَهُوَ الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ occurs amid God's guardianship until death, reinforcing divine rather than human possession of qahr.

luna: The section explicitly glosses the root س-ج-و as stillness and applies it to night. This verse calls night سَكَنًا, a settled time, while placing sun and moon in measured courses. | terra: وَجَعَلَ اللَّيْلَ سَكَنًا directly interprets night through rest, matching the section's dictionary statement that the night verb سجى is stillness.
terra: The Prophet is neither appointed guardian over idolaters nor manager of them, preparing the non-abusive speech boundary of 6:108.
terra: Believers must not insult rival objects of worship lest others insult God ignorantly, placing restraint on harsh speech even amid theological opposition.

luna: The verse forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity and commands fair measure. It extends the section's ban on overpowering an orphan to safeguarding his material rights. | terra: Approaching orphan property is forbidden except in the best manner until maturity, placing a strict boundary around the guardian's hand.
terra: The same threat of crosswise amputation and crucifixion makes Pharaoh's qahr bodily and punitive.

luna: The section cites Pharaoh's boast وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَاهِرُونَ as the human imitation of divine قهر. The verse supplies the tyrant's own claim of mastery over his people. | terra: Pharaoh's وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَاهِرُونَ follows his threat to kill sons and spare women, displaying human qahr as domination from above and degradation in practice.
terra: After Pharaoh claims qahr in 7:127, Moses tells his people to seek God's help and remain patient because the earth belongs to God, relocating mastery from tyrant to Lord.
terra: The same rescue formula recalls Pharaoh's slaughter and humiliation, making deliverance an escape from the hard tyrannical hand.
terra: The Messenger relieves people of their burdens and the shackles upon them, turning prophetic guidance into bodily and legal release.
terra: Humanity is created from one soul with its mate so that he may find rest with her, another relational form of the section's stillness.
terra: Take pardon, command what is recognized, and turn from the ignorant: the ayah gives a compact practice for refusing the rebuking tongue.
terra: God found the believers few, vulnerable, and afraid of being snatched, then فَآوَاكُمْ, strengthened them, and provided for them; shelter is the gentle answer to human domination.
terra: The assigned share of spoils includes kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers, protecting their provision even amid the hard scene of war.
terra: Even a hostile polytheist who seeks protection must be granted asylum and conveyed to safety; shelter and gentle hearing cross an enemy boundary.
terra: Amid battlefield flight, God sends His sakīnah upon the Messenger and believers before divine forces reverse the defeat; calm meets the source dictionary's defeated haste.
terra: حَتَّى يُعْطُوا الْجِزْيَةَ عَنْ يَدٍ وَهُمْ صَاغِرُونَ places the named giving root in a compelled political submission, a hard boundary to the source dictionary's willing, unresisting yield.
terra: In the exposed cave scene, God sends His سَكِينَة and unseen support; calm arrives precisely where fear and pursuit could force frantic flight.
terra: فَإِنْ أُعْطُوا مِنْهَا رَضُوا places أُعْطُوا and رَضُوا together as in 93:5, but exposes a merely conditional contentment governed by whether people receive alms.
terra: The better response to 9:58 is contentment with what God and His Messenger give and trust in further divine bounty, clarifying receiving without grasping resentment.
terra: Hypocrites وَيَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ, closing their hands while promoting wrong, a bodily image of withheld generosity.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to strive against disbelievers and hypocrites and be stern with them, a context-specific boundary to the gentleness commanded in 3:159.
terra: Believers are commanded to fight nearby hostile forces and let them find firmness in them, another contextual boundary to generalized softness.
terra: The Messenger is burdened by believers' suffering, deeply concerned for them, and رَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ, supplying the prophetic stance behind the gentle commands.

luna: The section's gloss of night as stillness is made explicit here: God made night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ, for people to rest in it, and day for seeing. | terra: God makes night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day visible, restating the section's night-and-day image in functional terms.
terra: Would the Prophet compel people until they became believers? The rhetorical question rejects coercion even in pursuit of faith.
terra: Noah asks whether he could force divine mercy upon unwilling hearers, rejecting coercion in the same dispute where elites want poor believers expelled.

luna: The section's dictionary note for ق-ل-ي includes driving a flock away. Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا when elite listeners want the believers gone, directly reversing that expulsive action. | terra: Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا to elites who despise his poor followers, a direct second prohibition of the section's chasing-away image.

luna: After Noah refuses to drive believers away in 11:29, he asks who could protect him from God if he did so. This verse contributes the accountability behind that refusal. | terra: After refusing to drive believers away in 11:29, Noah asks who could protect him from God if he did so, making non-expulsion a matter of accountability rather than courtesy.
terra: Noah's son says سَآوِي إِلَى جَبَلٍ, seeking self-shelter in a mountain, but the flood reveals that refuge without divine mercy cannot hold.
terra: Lot wishes for power or refuge in a strong support against the mob; the shelter root here names the secure backing sought under imminent coercion.
terra: عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ describes the Lord's uncut gift in the hereafter, extending the section's giving root into permanence.
terra: The Egyptian who buys Joseph tells his wife to honor his lodging and considers adopting him, turning a trafficked child toward household shelter.
terra: When Joseph reaches maturity, God gives him judgment and knowledge, completing the preservation begun by his honored lodging in 12:21.

luna: In prison, Joseph contrasts many lords with اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ. The same root named in the section locates ultimate mastery in God rather than in human dominators. | terra: Joseph asks whether scattered lords are better than Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ; the named root is again a divine title, not a human license.

luna: The section's root ء-و-ي includes tenderness toward someone; Joseph here takes his brother إِلَيْهِ and tells him not to grieve over what the others did. The sheltering gesture makes that tenderness concrete. | terra: آوَى إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ is Joseph's intimate reception of his brother; the named shelter root becomes a kinship gesture rather than mere lodging.
terra: Joseph's brothers arrive in distress with poor merchandise and ask him to give full measure and be charitable, a concrete scene of vulnerable petition.
terra: Joseph answers the brothers who once harmed him with “No blame upon you today” and prayer for forgiveness, the petition scene's strikingly gentle resolution.
terra: آوَى إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ depicts Joseph drawing his parents into his protection, meeting the parent-care scene of 17:23–24 through the section's shelter root.

luna: This verse calls God الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ while contrasting the Creator with powerless partners. It reinforces the section's distinction between divine قهر and human oppression. | terra: After contrasting creator with powerless partners, the ayah names God الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, reinforcing the section's Creator-servant boundary around qahr.
terra: أَلَا بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ locates settled rest in the heart, complementing the section's etymological heart-softening.
terra: Moses reminds Israel that divine favor rescued them from Pharaoh's degrading violence, explicitly setting blessing against oppression.
terra: A good word is likened to a good tree with firm root and high branches, making constructive speech a living, sheltering presence.
terra: The good tree continually gives fruit by its Lord's permission, showing the ongoing yield produced by the good word of 14:24.
terra: An evil word is like an uprooted tree with no stability, a direct reversal of the gentle word's rooted and fruitful effect.

luna: On the Day the earth is changed, the verse names God الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ. It places the root's absolute force in God's domain, the boundary the section draws against tyrannical humans. | terra: On the transformed earth all emerge before اللَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ; universal exposure gives the divine title its eschatological setting.
terra: فَاصْفَحِ الصَّفْحَ الْجَمِيلَ commands a beautiful overlooking, a deliberate release rather than a retaliatory hard hold.

luna: Alongside a warning not to strain one's eyes toward others' worldly gifts, this verse says to lower one's wing to believers. It joins the section's provision theme to humility toward people. | terra: وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ commands the Prophet to embody gentleness by lowering his wing to believers.
terra: Livestock carry burdens to places people could reach only with severe hardship, and the Lord is described as compassionate and merciful; serviceable animals embody softened difficulty.
terra: Whatever blessing people possess is from God, locating the section's named niʿmah root wholly in divine provision.
terra: God makes homes places of rest and livestock hides into light, portable dwellings, concretizing shelter, ease, and compliant animals in one provision scene.
terra: God commands justice, excellence, and giving to kin while forbidding oppression; gift and coercion are placed on opposite sides of one compact command.
terra: A town secure and tranquil, with abundant provision, denies God's favors and loses its ease; the named blessing root is tested through gratitude rather than possession.

luna: The instruction to invite with wisdom and good exhortation and to argue in the best manner makes measured speech an explicit religious stance, echoing the section's gentle word even to Pharaoh. | terra: Invitation is to proceed with wisdom, good instruction, and argument بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ, specifying the verbal manner developed in 20:44.

luna: For retaliation, the verse permits only equal measure and says patience is better. It sets a limit on the overpowering response that the section's account of قهر warns against. | terra: Retaliation may match the harm suffered, yet patience is expressly better; the ayah draws a boundary around force after the gentle invitation of 16:125.
terra: The patience preferred in 16:126 is possible only through God, and the Prophet must not grieve or feel constricted by opponents' schemes.
terra: The Lord extends support to both groups, and وَمَا كَانَ عَطَاءُ رَبِّكَ مَحْظُورًا declares His giving unconfined, the opposite of a clenched human distribution.

luna: The source section names the root ن-ه-ر for harsh rebuke; 17:23 uses تَنْهَرْهُمَا to forbid scolding parents and replaces it with a gracious word, extending the ban on the hard verbal grip to the home. | terra: This is the only other imperative use of the section's rebuking verb: وَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا forbids scolding aged parents and replaces it with قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا, making gentle speech the positive counterpart.

luna: The section contrasts قهر, lowering another person, with lowering one's own wing. Here the wing is lowered to parents out of mercy, and the verse asks for mercy in return for their raising the speaker as a child. | terra: After 17:23 forbids verbal harshness, the body answers with وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ; one lowers oneself mercifully rather than lowering another through qahr.
terra: Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due supplies the material setting for the easy word commanded two ayat later in 17:28.

luna: The section cites this exact case: when turning away from people whose request one cannot meet, give them قَوْلًا مَيْسُورًا, an easy word. It makes gentle speech the response even when provision is unavailable. | terra: When material help must be deferred, فَقُلْ لَهُمْ قَوْلًا مَيْسُورًا requires an easy, consoling word; it directly joins the section's giving hand to its speaking tongue.
terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit; the ayah gives the section's “hold” a measured ethical boundary.
terra: Immediately after the measured-hand command of 17:29, the Lord expands and restricts provision with full knowledge, distinguishing divine measure from human stinginess.

luna: The verse forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity. It makes the section's prohibition on crushing an orphan apply to the handling of his property too. | terra: The same “best manner until maturity” rule protects orphan property, followed by the demand to fulfill covenants.

luna: The verse forbids walking on earth with arrogance. This is a specific contrary gait to the section's dictionary gloss of ه-د-ي as calm, well-conducted walking. | terra: وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا forbids an exultant, dominating gait, supplying a bodily contrast to calm guidance.

luna: The verse tells the Prophet's servants to say what is أَحْسَنُ, because Satan sows discord between them. It parallels the section's replacement of harsh rebuke with words that do not wound. | terra: God tells His servants يَقُولُوا الَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ because Satan incites discord, identifying careful speech as the restraint that prevents verbal harm.

luna: The youths take refuge in the cave, أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, and ask God for mercy and right guidance. It repeats the section's sheltering-a-vulnerable-person image through the same refuge root it discusses. | terra: The youths أَوَوْا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ and ask for mercy and right guidance, bringing shelter, softened divine care, and direction together.

luna: The youths are told to take refuge in the cave, فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, where their Lord will spread mercy and ease their affair. This gives the shelter image an explicit movement from protection to mercy. | terra: فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ leads immediately to promised mercy and مِرْفَقًا, a facilitated outcome; shelter, tenderness, and ease converge exactly as in the section's lexicon.

luna: The verse commands patience with those who call on their Lord morning and evening and forbids turning one's eyes from them for worldly adornment. It echoes 6:52's humble callers and opposes status-based exclusion. | terra: The Prophet must patiently keep himself with those who call on their Lord morning and evening and not let his eyes pass beyond them, a sustained gentle hold parallel to 6:52.

luna: The story explains that the wall protected treasure belonging to two orphans until they matured, by mercy from their Lord. This is a concrete image of sheltering vulnerable children and guarding what is theirs, opposite to قهر. | terra: A wall preserves treasure for two orphan boys until maturity, explicitly as mercy from the Lord; unseen protection answers the orphan's vulnerability without crushing control.
terra: John is بَرًّا بِوَالِدَيْهِ and not جَبَّارًا عَصِيًّا; kindness to parents is explicitly opposed to tyrannical character.
terra: Jesus says God made him dutiful to his mother and not جَبَّارًا شَقِيًّا, repeating the boundary between filial gentleness and coercive arrogance.
terra: فَلَا تَعْجَلْ عَلَيْهِمْ restrains haste toward deniers because their term is already counted, a judicial form of the section's unhurried posture.
terra: The infant Moses is cast into the chest and river, taken by an enemy, yet covered with divine love and formed under God's eye; a dangerous “casting away” becomes preserving care.
terra: Moses' sister leads to a caregiver, and God returns him to his mother so her eyes may be comforted, completing the infant's sheltered recovery.
terra: The command “Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed” identifies the violent addressee before 20:44 requires gentle speech, showing that softness is deliberate even toward tyranny.

luna: The section cites the command to Moses and Aaron to address Pharaoh with قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا. Even this ruler is approached with a soft word, sharpening the contrast with the section's forbidden harsh speech. | terra: Even Pharaoh is to be addressed with قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا, the clearest limit placed on the tongue's impulse to rebuke.
terra: Moses describes the Lord as الَّذِي أَعْطَى كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هَدَى, placing the section's two named roots, giving and guiding, in the same divine sequence.
terra: Pharaoh threatens to cut opposing hands and feet and crucify the magicians, displaying the coercive hand behind his claim to mastery.
terra: وَلَا تَعْجَلْ بِالْقُرْآنِ directly repeats the source dictionary's wording “do not hurry,” addressing the Prophet with restraint until revelation is completed.
terra: The Prophet is told to glorify God before sunrise, before sunset, and during the night so that he may be satisfied; daily light and darkness culminate in the same رضى promised in 93:5.
terra: When wrongdoers sense divine might, إِذَا هُمْ مِنْهَا يَرْكُضُونَ pictures frantic running in defeat, the exact motion opposed by the source dictionary's calm gait.
terra: لَا تَرْكُضُوا commands those fleeing judgment not to run, sharply reversing their defeated haste and echoing the section's “do not hurry.”
terra: Humanity is created of haste and told فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُونِ; this names the temperament against which the section's lexical softness is heard.
terra: The saved are guided to wholesome speech and to the path of the Praiseworthy, placing the section's guidance root directly beside good words.
terra: Sacrificial cattle are made serviceable, stand quietly, and then feed الْقَانِعَ وَالْمُعْتَرَّ; this concretizes both the source dictionary's yielding camel and care for one who comes asking.
terra: After the yielding cattle and feeding in 22:36, their flesh and blood do not reach God; piety does, and their being subjected should lead to magnifying God for guidance.
terra: Satanic suggestion becomes a trial for diseased and hardened hearts, again making hardness the condition that distorts reception.
terra: Those given knowledge recognize the truth and their hearts become humbly receptive to it, supplying the softened counterpart to 22:53.
terra: God has placed no constricting hardship in religion; the ayah makes non-oppressive religious obligation part of Abraham's inherited path.
terra: وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَى رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ portrays divine shelter of mother and son as a settled, provisioned refuge.

luna: This command also says to repel evil with what is best. In its own context it asks God to ward off the opponents' descriptions, extending the section's soft-response principle to hostile speech. | terra: ادْفَعْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ directs the Prophet to meet evil with what is better, turning resistance away from matching hardness.
terra: People of means must not swear to stop giving kin, the needy, and emigrants; pardon and overlooking replace the closed hand and wounded relation.

luna: The verse makes night a covering, sleep a rest, and day a time of rising/spreading. It expands the section's quiet-night and dawn pairing into the body's rest and return to activity. | terra: Night is clothing, sleep repose, and day a rising, giving the section's still night an enveloping and restorative interpretation.

luna: The servants of the Merciful walk humbly, and answer ignorant address with سَلَامًا. It joins the section's calm-walking sense to a non-harsh verbal response. | terra: The servants of the Merciful يَمْشُونَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ هَوْنًا and answer ignorant address with peace, uniting the section's unhurried gait and gentle tongue in one ayah.
terra: The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily but keep a measured middle course, giving the open hand a disciplined balance.
terra: Pharaoh answers Moses' proclamation by threatening prison, a coercive verbal response that exposes the regime addressed with gentle speech.
terra: Pharaoh again threatens crosswise amputation and crucifixion when belief escapes his control, a repeated hard grasp on conscience and body.

luna: The leaders call Noah's followers “the lowliest” just before Noah refuses to drive believers away in 26:114. This verse supplies the status contempt that presses against the section's command not to put down the vulnerable.

luna: Noah repeats that he is not one to drive believers away. In its own exchange, this verse rejects the social exclusion the section's secondary flock-driving sense and its ban on hard treatment illuminate. | terra: Noah again states وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ, refusing to purchase elite approval by driving vulnerable believers away.
terra: وَإِذَا بَطَشْتُمْ بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ names violent seizing performed as tyrants, perhaps the clearest nonlexical picture of the section's hard hand.

luna: The verse says وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ to believers who follow the Prophet. It repeats the section's image of lowering one's own wing, the bodily opposite of forcing another down. | terra: وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِمَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ repeats the lowered-wing posture for the Prophet's followers, a bodily opposite to qahr from above.
terra: God is the One who answers the distressed caller and removes harm, turning supplication into relief rather than humiliation.

luna: This verse likewise says night was made لِيَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day made bright for sight. It repeats the settled-night scene that the section draws from 93:2. | terra: Night is made so people may rest and day to give sight, repeating the quiet-night relation that the section hears in سجى.
terra: Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the population, weakens a group, and slaughters its sons; the ayah unfolds domination plus degradation, the section's definition of qahr.
terra: Moses' mother is told to nurse him, cast him into the river only when afraid, and neither fear nor grieve because God will return him; tenderness and trust frame the release.
terra: Pharaoh's household picks up the infant who will become their enemy, identifying the threatening house into which the vulnerable child is received.
terra: Pharaoh's wife says “Do not kill him” and proposes benefit or adoption, a gentle protective intervention inside the tyrant's household.
terra: When Moses refuses other nurses, his sister guides the household to a family who will care for him sincerely, supplying the practical shelter he needs.
terra: God returns Moses to his mother so her eye is comforted and she no longer grieves, fulfilling the soft promise of 28:7.
terra: After Moses reaches to seize a man, he is accused of wanting to be جَبَّارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ; the scene ties a grasping hand to tyrannical domination.

luna: The two women hold their flock back until the shepherds leave and explain that their father is old. This specific vulnerable-flock scene connects to the section's secondary account of driving a herd and its concern for a gentle response to someone in need.
luna: After the women's explanation in 28:23, this verse says Moses watered for them and then withdrew to shade. Its own contribution is practical help for people whose need he has just heard.
terra: When believers hear vain or hurtful talk, they turn away and say peace rather than return the verbal aggression.
terra: The question asks who besides God could bring a night in which people rest if day were perpetual, making stillness a necessary mercy.

luna: The verse names night as a time for rest and day as a time to seek God's bounty. It joins the section's settled night with its soft-giving and ease-in-living details. | terra: Divine mercy makes night and day so people may rest in one and seek bounty in the other, joining repose, provision, and gratitude.

luna: The instruction is to argue with the People of the Book in the best manner, except those who act unjustly. It gives another explicit boundary for measured speech alongside the section's soft word to Pharaoh and its ban on rebuking the asker. | terra: Disputation with the People of the Book must use what is best, except toward those who act unjustly, a stated boundary for gentle address.
terra: Spouses are created so one may find tranquility with the other, and affection and mercy are placed between them; a close human bond is defined by gentle repose.
terra: Sleep by night and day and seeking divine bounty are both signs, loosening the rigid equation of night with rest while preserving repose and provision.
terra: فَآتِ ذَا الْقُرْبَى حَقَّهُ وَالْمِسْكِينَ وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ again frames aid as a recipient's due, not the giver's humiliating favor.

luna: This verse forbids turning one's cheek in contempt and walking on earth arrogantly. It supplies the proud bodily stance opposite to the section's calm, yielding walk and its refusal to put others down. | terra: Do not turn the cheek from people or walk boastfully; this identifies the proud posture corrected by measured gait and lowered voice in 31:19.

luna: The following verse tells the listener to وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ and lower the voice. Its measured gait and speech echo the section's dictionary note for ه-د-ي as calm walking and its contrast with harsh speech. | terra: وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ وَاغْضُضْ مِنْ صَوْتِكَ pairs measured walking with a lowered voice, then contrasts the harshest voice with a donkey's bray.
terra: God has lavished apparent and hidden favors upon people, broadening the named blessing root from visible ease to unseen care.
terra: One who yields his face to God while doing good has اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَى; yielding and a secure handhold coexist without the humiliation of human qahr.
terra: When fear passes, hypocrites سَلَقُوكُمْ بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ, lashing believers with sharp tongues; the hard tongue becomes almost a weapon.

luna: The verse warns the Prophet's wives not to soften their speech in a way that invites desire from a sick-hearted listener, while commanding an appropriate word. This is a contextual boundary on the section's soft-speech image, which is directed toward the vulnerable and even toward Pharaoh. | terra: Prophetic wives are told not to be yieldingly soft in speech where it could invite diseased desire, but to speak appropriately; softness itself needs a moral setting.
terra: When marriage ends before consummation, women are to be provided for and released graciously, another gentle rule for letting go rather than retaining control.
terra: Believers are commanded to fear God and speak a straight, sound word, another positive discipline placed on the tongue.
terra: وَذَلَّلْنَاهَا لَهُمْ describes cattle made docile so some become mounts and others food, directly recalling the source dictionary's compliant camel.
terra: Jonah is cast onto the bare shore while sick, the exposed condition that divine favor in 68:49 prevents from becoming blameworthy abandonment.
terra: God grows a spreading gourd over Jonah, adding bodily shade and shelter to the exposed shore scene of 37:145.
terra: هَذَا عَطَاؤُنَا فَامْنُنْ أَوْ أَمْسِكْ names divine gift and then gives Solomon discretion to bestow or withhold, placing giving and holding in one explicit formula.

luna: The declaration that there is no god but Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ repeats the root in the section's divine-authority contrast. | terra: The Prophet is told to announce that there is no deity but اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, joining warning speech to exclusive divine qahr.

luna: Rejecting the claim that God takes a child, this verse names Him الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ. Its context again makes the section's root belong to God's unique sovereignty. | terra: The rejection of divine offspring closes with سُبْحَانَهُ هُوَ اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, again reserving the title for God.
terra: Those who listen to speech and follow its best are precisely those God has guided, joining verbal discernment to the named guidance root.
terra: Woe is pronounced on hearts hardened against God's remembrance, preparing the explicit softening of skins and hearts in 39:23.
terra: After bodies shiver in awe, تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ softens skins and hearts toward God's remembrance, giving Qur'anic form to the section's softened heart.
terra: The Prophet receives the Book for people, but whoever strays does so against himself and the Prophet is not their manager.

luna: At the gathering when the hidden is exposed, the verse says dominion belongs to Allah الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ. It anchors the section's contrast between God's power and a human's domination. | terra: On the day all are exposed, sovereignty is declared to belong to اللَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ, placing irresistible domination at final judgment.
terra: “Call upon Me; I will answer you” positively invites petition, the opposite of meeting the asker with verbal rejection.

luna: The verse calls night a time لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day a time of sight, then names this as God's favor. It gives another direct formulation of the section's still-night image. | terra: God makes night for rest and day for sight, then describes His bounty, joining repose to divine favor.
terra: The best speech belongs to one who calls to God, acts rightly, and declares submission, defining excellence of speech through invitation rather than rebuke.

luna: The verse commands دفع evil with what is better, saying that an enemy may become like a close friend. It gives a specific response to hostility opposite to answering with a harsh verbal grip. | terra: ادْفَعْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ turns hostile relation into intimate friendship; the ayah makes a better response, rather than a harder counterblow, transformative.
terra: After evil is repelled with what is better in 41:34, this response is said to be received only by the patient and greatly fortunate; patient restraint is what sustains the gentle answer.
terra: The One holding the keys of heaven and earth expands and restricts provision, assigning ultimate opening and tightening to divine knowledge.
terra: Those who avoid grave wrongs forgive when angered, making release at the moment of provocation a mark of faithful character.

luna: The verse bounds retaliation for an injury by equivalence, then commends pardon and reconciliation. It clarifies the difference between just redress and the domineering, humiliating grip the section prohibits. | terra: A wrong may receive an equal response, but pardon and reconciliation bring reward from God, balancing justice with the gentler release of grievance.
terra: Patient endurance and forgiveness are described as matters of firm resolve, elevating gentle release above reactive hardness.
terra: If hearers turn away, the Prophet has not been sent as their guardian; his task is conveyance, not controlling their response.
terra: The Prophet did not know the Book or faith until revelation became a light by which God guides; this is another direct divine account of prophetic guidance.

luna: The section's dictionary note for ع-ط-و describes an obedient, nonresisting camel and a pliant bow. This verse describes mounts made subservient and asks riders to remember God's favor when they settle on them. | terra: Settling on the backs of ships and cattle prompts remembrance of the One who made them serviceable, turning mastery over an animal into gratitude rather than cruelty.
terra: فَاسْتَخَفَّ قَوْمَهُ فَأَطَاعُوهُ shows Pharaoh making his people contemptibly light until they obey, matching qahr's combination of domination and degradation.
terra: فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ وَقُلْ سَلَامٌ joins release of grievance to a peaceful word, a concise opposite to nahr.
terra: وَنَعْمَةٍ كَانُوا فِيهَا فَاكِهِينَ names the comfortable ease Pharaoh's people enjoyed before losing it, close to the source dictionary's “ease in living.”
terra: The Messenger must endure with the resolve of earlier messengers and وَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلْ لَهُمْ, applying the source's “do not hurry” to judgment against opponents.
terra: When people are called to spend, some withhold; the ayah says the withholder is withholding only from himself, exposing the closed hand's self-defeat.
terra: هُوَ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ السَّكِينَةَ فِي قُلُوبِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ locates divine calm inside hearts, the inward form of the section's gentle hold.
terra: At the pledge beneath the tree, God knows what is in believers' hearts and sends السَّكِينَةَ عَلَيْهِمْ, joining a bodily pledge to inward composure.
terra: Unbelievers put heated zealotry in their hearts, while God sends His sakīnah upon the Messenger and believers; the ayah explicitly stages the two opposed inner grips.
terra: أَشِدَّاءُ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ similarly distinguishes severity toward hostile opposition from mercy within the believing community.
terra: Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's or address him loudly like one another, setting a limit on forceful vocal manner.
terra: Those who lower their voices before God's Messenger are praised, giving the preceding prohibition a positive form of vocal restraint.
terra: Ridicule, mutual defamation, and insulting names are forbidden, specifying ordinary verbal forms of demeaning another.
terra: وَمَا أَنْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِجَبَّارٍ denies that the Prophet is a coercive dominator and directs him instead to remind through the Qur'an.

luna: The verse gives the poor asker and deprived person a known share in the giving community's wealth. That standing makes the section's command not to rebuke the asker concrete. | terra: وَفِي أَمْوَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ makes the asker and the one unable to ask both rightful recipients, moving response beyond discretionary condescension.

terra: The source dictionary's flexible قَوْس appears as the section's object; فَكَانَ قَابَ قَوْسَيْنِ uses bow-lengths only as a measure of nearness, so the link is lexical and spatial rather than a claim about flexibility.
terra: وَأَعْطَى قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَى uses the named giving root for a small gift abruptly stopped, showing a hand that opens only to harden again.
terra: Noah is called mad and وَازْدُجِرَ, “rebuked/driven off” with the same z-j-r wording used in the source dictionary to define harsh nahr.
terra: فَتَعَاطَى فَعَقَرَ uses a different stem of the section's named ع ط و root for the culprit's reaching/undertaking before hamstringing the she-camel, a violent reversal of yielding gift.
terra: God hears the woman who pleads with the Prophet and complains to Him, giving a vulnerable speaker divine attention rather than rebuke.
terra: Believers must make room for one another in gatherings and rise when asked; social space is handled through accommodation rather than status pressure.
terra: The distribution to kin, orphans, needy, and travelers is designed so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, an institutional check on the closed hand.
terra: The Helpers prefer others even while needy themselves, and success belongs to those protected from the soul's stinginess; generous reception overcomes the inner hard grip.
terra: Listening, obeying, and spending are joined to protection from the soul's stinginess, again locating the obstruction to giving within the self.
terra: Divorced women must be housed according to means, not harmed to constrict them, and nursing arrangements settled بِمَعْرُوفٍ; shelter, provision, and humane speech oppose coercive pressure.
terra: The well-off and constrained alike give from what God gave them, while God burdens no soul beyond His gift and promises ease after hardship.
terra: The angels over the Fire are described as harsh and stern and never disobey God, a divinely assigned context where hardness serves judgment rather than ego.
terra: The repeated command to be stern toward disbelievers and hypocrites prevents the section's softness from being read as the erasure of every moral boundary.
terra: By the Lord's blessing, the Prophet is not mad; divine niʿmah directly answers a degrading verbal accusation aimed at him.
terra: The Prophet must not obey a habitual, contemptible swearer; the passage begins a portrait of corrosive speech and hard character.
terra: The same figure is a fault-finder who moves about spreading slander, specifying the rebuking tongue as a settled social practice.
terra: He obstructs good, transgresses, and sins, joining the harmful tongue to a hand that prevents benefit from reaching others.
terra: His character is further marked as cruel and ignoble, completing the passage's concentrated opposite to gentleness.
terra: The Prophet must patiently await his Lord's judgment and not repeat Jonah's distressed reaction; this prepares for the preserving divine favor in 68:49.
terra: نِعْمَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِ catches Jonah before he is cast onto the open shore blameworthy, making divine favor a preserving hold against rejection.
terra: فَهُوَ فِي عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ gives the section's “comfortable life” a final-life form explicitly joined to satisfaction.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to exercise beautiful patience, a composed response to pressure consistent with the section's calm bearing.
terra: The fleeing sinner would ransom even فَصِيلَتِهِ الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ, identifying one's close clan by its ordinary work of sheltering.

luna: The verse describes a known right in the wealth for people who ask and those deprived. It treats the asker as a rightful recipient, complementing the section's ban on answering him harshly. | terra: Believers set aside a recognized share in their wealth, preparing the material answer to the two vulnerable recipients named in 70:25.

luna: This completes the preceding description by naming the recipients as السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ. The asker in the section is thus part of a repeated Quranic scene of provision. | terra: That recognized share is لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ, directly converting the encounter with an asker into acknowledged right.
terra: The source dictionary gloss for wadāʿ invokes وَقَار; مَا لَكُمْ لَا تَرْجُونَ لِلَّهِ وَقَارًا uses that form for due majesty or dignity, a different but relevant edge of composed gravity.

luna: The Prophet is told to endure what people say and leave them with a graceful parting. That measured response contrasts with the harsh verbal grip named in the section. | terra: The Prophet must bear what opponents say and leave them هَجْرًا جَمِيلًا, answering verbal injury with patient, dignified disengagement.
terra: God tells the Prophet to leave affluent deniers, أُولِي النَّعْمَةِ, to Him and grant them a little respite; luxury from the named root is paired with unhurried judgment.
terra: لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِ لِسَانَكَ لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِ applies “do not hurry” to the Prophet's tongue itself, turning gentleness into measured reception and recitation.
terra: After forbidding the Prophet's hurried tongue in 75:16, God assumes responsibility for collecting and reciting the revelation, replacing anxious grasping with trustful reception.
terra: Once God recites the revelation, the Prophet is to follow its recitation; measured following is the positive movement opposite haste.

luna: The righteous feed the needy, the orphan, and the captive despite their own love of the food. It turns the section's soft hand toward vulnerable recipients into a concrete act of care. | terra: They feed, despite loving the food, the needy, orphan, and captive; even a captive receives the open hand rather than domination.

luna: The next verse says they seek neither repayment nor thanks for feeding them. It completes the feeding scene with a giving stance free of leverage over its recipients. | terra: The feeders seek neither repayment nor thanks, removing the verbal and social pressure that can turn a gift into hard control.
terra: وَجَعَلْنَا نَوْمَكُمْ سُبَاتًا supplies the repose within the following night-and-day sequence.
terra: وَجَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا makes night an enveloping cover rather than an abandonment, continuing the repose of 78:9.
terra: وَجَعَلْنَا النَّهَارَ مَعَاشًا completes the calm night's counterpart with the day's livelihood, paralleling the section's paired times and comfortable life.
terra: عَطَاءً حِسَابًا names the hereafter's ample recompense as a gift from the Lord, another direct occurrence of the section's giving root.
terra: “Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed” identifies the tyrant who is nevertheless approached through the measured invitation in 79:18–19.
terra: Moses asks Pharaoh هَلْ لَكَ إِلَى أَنْ تَزَكَّى, a question offering purification rather than opening with rebuke.
terra: وَأَهْدِيَكَ إِلَى رَبِّكَ joins guidance to that gentle invitation, showing what the soft word of 20:44 is meant to accomplish.
terra: Pharaoh proclaims himself the highest lord, making explicit the usurped supremacy behind his human qahr.
terra: God seizes Pharaoh in exemplary punishment for his latter and former offenses, contrasting the tyrant's grasp with final divine seizure.

luna: The section's dictionary note for the root ض-ح-و says it carries the sense of not hurrying; 79:29 brings out the earth's ضُحَاهَا after darkening its night, repeating the dawn-and-night scene behind the section's opening. | terra: وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَاهَا uses the named root for the earth's brought-forth daylight, another Qur'anic sense beside the source dictionary's gentle, unhurried branch.

luna: The opening describes a man who عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ when a blind person came. Though the visitor is a seeker rather than clearly the material petitioner of 93:10, the scene warns against a brusque response to someone approaching in need. | terra: عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّى records a facial and bodily withdrawal, the opposite of a gentle reception for one who approaches.

luna: The next verse identifies the visitor as the blind man. This completes the encounter behind the frown and turn in 80:1, a concrete counterpart to the section's concern for a vulnerable asker. | terra: أَنْ جَاءَهُ الْأَعْمَى identifies the disregarded visitor as a blind man, sharpening the vulnerable-asker parallel.
terra: The overlooked visitor might have purified himself, showing what is lost when surface status controls the response.
terra: He might have remembered and benefited from the reminder; his request carried spiritual value rather than nuisance.
terra: أَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَى turns to the self-sufficient person, establishing the social contrast governing the mistaken attention.
terra: فَأَنْتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى says the self-sufficient one received deliberate attention, unlike the vulnerable visitor.
terra: The Prophet bears no blame if that self-sufficient hearer does not purify himself, removing the rationale for preferential pursuit.

luna: The passage later describes another person who جَاءَكَ يَسْعَىٰ, coming to the Prophet with effort. It brings a seeker into the same scene of attention and neglect that illuminates the section's treatment of the asker. | terra: وَأَمَّا مَنْ جَاءَكَ يَسْعَى returns to the seeker who came striving, a concrete counterpart to the section's sāʾil.

luna: This seeker is described as one who fears, giving a reason to attend to him rather than overlook him. It echoes the section's refusal to dismiss a supplicant harshly. | terra: وَهُوَ يَخْشَى reveals the seeker's inward reverence and further reverses the status judgment.

luna: The passage says the Prophet is distracted from that seeker. This completes the warning in 80:1–2 about turning away, a neglectful boundary related to the section's prohibition on rebuking the asker. | terra: فَأَنْتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّى completes the rebuke: distraction from the earnest vulnerable seeker is itself the failed hold.
terra: وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى is a divine promise to ease the Prophet toward ease, close to the section's yielding roots and unforced movement.
terra: وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَاعِمَةٌ gives the section's dictionary sense of the niʿmah root—soft, at ease—a bodily appearance.
terra: لِسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ joins satisfaction to the “soft/at-ease” faces of 88:8, echoing the gift-and-contentment movement of 93:5.
terra: فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنْتَ مُذَكِّرٌ defines the messenger's task as reminder rather than crushing control.
terra: لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُصَيْطِرٍ explicitly denies mastery over hearers, completing 88:21's boundary on prophetic force.
terra: When God gives expansively, the human says He أَكْرَمَنِي and the ayah uses وَنَعَّمَهُ; the named softness/blessing root is tested by what follows toward the orphan.
terra: The same person reads measured provision as humiliation, exposing the mistaken equation of a tightened livelihood with divine contempt before the orphan indictment.

luna: The passage condemns failing to honor the orphan. This directly reverses the respect and shelter implied by the section's account of finding the Prophet an orphan and providing for him. | terra: كَلَّا بَلْ لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ corrects the wealth-based reasoning of 89:15–16 by making treatment of the orphan the test of bestowed ease.

luna: The next failure is not urging the feeding of the poor. It places provision for the needy beside the section's gift and its restraint toward the asker. | terra: وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ extends that failure from the orphan to the unfed poor.

luna: The passage then condemns devouring inheritance greedily. This supplies a material form of the hard grip against the vulnerable that the section forbids. | terra: وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَمًّا shows the grasping appetite that accompanies neglect of orphan and poor.
terra: وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا names attachment to accumulated wealth as the inner hard grip behind the preceding failures.
terra: يَا أَيَّتُهَا النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ addresses the soul defined by settled calm, the inward culmination of the section's recurrent stillness.
terra: ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً joins that tranquility to mutual satisfaction, strengthening the relation between calm and contentment.
terra: فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ makes loosening a human neck, the undoing of a hard physical hold, the first form of the steep moral path.
terra: أَوْ إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ adds feeding under famine to the release of 90:13.

luna: The steep path includes feeding an orphan who is near of kin. This is a concrete caring act toward the very vulnerable figure whom the section says not to overpower. | terra: The feeding is directed to يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ, making the section's orphan a concrete recipient of costly care.

luna: The next act is feeding a needy person in the dust, bringing the section's treatment of the asker beside provision for someone in visible need. | terra: أَوْ مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ extends that care to the destitute person brought low to the dust.

luna: After the feeding acts in 90:15–16, this verse names those who believe and counsel one another to compassion. It gives the care scene its communal quality. | terra: The sequence culminates in mutual counsel to patience and مَرْحَمَةِ, naming mercy as the social bond behind freeing and feeding.
terra: وَالشَّمْسِ وَضُحَاهَا repeats the section's ḍuḥā word as the sun's brightness, anchoring its secondary “do not hurry” reading in the word's ordinary luminous scene.
terra: وَالنَّهَارِ إِذَا جَلَّاهَا develops the daylight side of 91:1 and parallels the section's opening movement from ḍuḥā.
terra: وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا sets covering night against revealed day, a second oath-pair that helps distinguish visual covering from the section's still night.
terra: God's messenger warns the people concerning نَاقَةَ اللَّهِ وَسُقْيَاهَا, placing a protected she-camel and its drink before their violent act.
terra: They deny and hamstring the she-camel, the hard human action against the animal set apart in 91:13.

luna: This verse uses أَعْطَى, the same giving root named in the section, for one who gives and is mindful. It makes the section's yielding, generous hand an ethical act. | terra: فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَى وَاتَّقَى makes the section's named giving root the first movement toward an eased path.
terra: The giver of 92:5 also affirms the finest promise; that receptive assent is the inward yielding that leads to ease in 92:7.

luna: The ease promised after the giving in 92:5 is stated as فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى. It links the section's soft giving and its dictionary sense of ease in living to a path made easy. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى states the ease opened for the giver of 92:5, developing the yielding quality the section hears in أَعْطَى.

luna: This is the opposing branch to 92:5: the person who withholds and sees himself as self-sufficient receives the hard way, reversing the section's image of soft, yielding giving. | terra: وَأَمَّا مَنْ بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَى reverses the giving of 92:5 through withholding and felt self-sufficiency.
terra: The self-sufficient withholder denies the finest promise, supplying the inward refusal that leads to the difficult path in 92:10.

luna: After the withholding and denial described in 92:8–9, this verse says the hard way will be made easy for that person. It completes the contrast to 92:5–7's giving and eased path. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَى makes the withholder's destination “difficulty,” the formal opposite of the giver's ease in 92:7.
terra: The one who يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ يَتَزَكَّى gives wealth for purification, supplying the concrete generous act that culminates in satisfaction at 92:21.
terra: وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَى closely echoes the promise of future satisfaction in 93:5, while the preceding scene makes generous giving its setting.
terra: فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا is a direct divine assurance to the Prophet that ease accompanies hardship, close to the section's yielding and restful semantic field.
terra: The repeated assurance that ease accompanies hardship makes gentleness and facilitation emphatic rather than incidental.
terra: فَهُوَ فِي عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ repeats the pleasing life, a concise Qur'anic counterpart to the dictionary's ease and repose in living.
terra: Woe is pronounced on every slanderer and mocker, the character built from the harsh tongue the section forbids.

luna: The denier of judgment is described as يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ, roughly thrusting the orphan away. This is a direct contrary action to the section's ban on overpowering him. | terra: فَذَلِكَ الَّذِي يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ pictures the orphan being shoved away, the stark physical opposite of the ban on crushing him.

luna: The next verse condemns failing to urge feeding the poor. It completes the orphan's rejection with neglect of provision, against the section's gentle treatment and giving image. | terra: The one who shoves the orphan also fails to urge feeding the poor, joining a hard hand to withheld provision.
terra: إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ الْكَوْثَرَ is another direct divine address to the Prophet with the section's giving root, but here the gift is already emphatically bestowed.
